title: Everyday steps that may lower cancer risk
summary: Evidence-backed habits may reduce the risk of some cancers, but no routine can prevent every cancer.
author: CareGuide Editorial Team

content.heading: Small steps, not guarantees
paragraphs: Research suggests that some everyday choices can lower the chance of developing certain cancers. These are population-level findings, not a way to predict what will happen to one person. Cancer has many causes, and many cases cannot be prevented.

content.heading: Habits supported by prevention guidance
paragraphs: The World Cancer Research Fund recommends being physically active, maintaining a healthy weight where possible, eating a varied diet with wholegrains, vegetables, fruit and beans, and limiting alcohol and processed meat. Avoiding tobacco and protecting skin from excessive ultraviolet exposure are also important.
items: If you smoke, ask a health professional about practical support to stop.
Choose activity and food changes that are realistic for your health, culture and circumstances.
Ask a qualified health worker whether recommended vaccines or screening services apply to you.

content.heading: Make changes with support
paragraphs: These steps do not replace medical care and cannot guarantee that cancer will be avoided. A clinician can help adapt advice to your health needs. If you have a new or persistent symptom, arrange an assessment rather than waiting for lifestyle changes to help.

title: Food and cancer: what the evidence can and cannot tell us
summary: A balanced eating pattern can support health; no single food is a cancer cure or a guarantee of prevention.
author: CareGuide Editorial Team

content.heading: Look at overall patterns
paragraphs: Research suggests that dietary patterns can influence the risk of some cancers, but studies do not let us predict an individual's outcome from one meal or ingredient. The World Cancer Research Fund recommends including wholegrains, vegetables, fruit and beans as part of a varied diet.

content.heading: Keep claims in perspective
paragraphs: Guidance also recommends limiting red and processed meat, fast foods and sugar-sweetened drinks. This is not a claim that a particular food directly causes cancer in every person. No food, supplement or diet has been shown to cure cancer, and supplements should not be used for cancer prevention unless a clinician advises them for another reason.

content.heading: Choose changes that work for you
paragraphs: Food access, health conditions, culture and personal preferences all matter. Aim for practical changes rather than restrictive diets, and speak with a qualified health professional before making major changes, especially during cancer treatment.

sources.title: How to eat a balanced diet

title: Warning signs: when a change deserves attention
summary: Many warning signs have non-cancer causes, but persistent or unusual changes should be discussed with a health professional.
author: CareGuide Editorial Team

content.heading: Notice changes that are new or persistent
paragraphs: Possible warning signs can include a new lump, unexplained weight loss, unusual bleeding, a changing mole, a cough that does not improve, ongoing fatigue, or changes in bowel or bladder habits. This list is not complete, and the same symptoms can have many causes.

content.heading: Arrange an assessment
paragraphs: Contact a qualified health worker about symptoms that are new, persistent, getting worse, or worrying you. Do not wait for a symptom checker or an article to decide whether you need care. A clinician can ask questions, examine you and decide whether tests are appropriate.

content.heading: Seek urgent help for severe symptoms
paragraphs: For severe, sudden or rapidly worsening symptoms, or if you feel seriously unwell, seek urgent medical help using local emergency services. This article cannot assess urgency for an individual.

title: Screening and check-ups: what to ask your clinician
summary: Screening recommendations vary by test and location; a clinician can help you understand what is appropriate for you.
author: CareGuide Editorial Team

content.heading: Screening is not the same as checking symptoms
paragraphs: Screening tests look for certain cancers or precancerous changes in people who may not have symptoms. If you already have a concerning symptom, ask for a clinical assessment rather than waiting for a routine screening appointment.

content.heading: Recommendations depend on context
paragraphs: Which tests are recommended, and at what ages or intervals, depends on the cancer, available local services, personal and family history, and current national guidance. Screening can have benefits and possible harms, so it is important to understand both before deciding.
items: Ask which screening tests are recommended where you live and why.
Mention relevant family history, previous diagnoses and any current symptoms.
Ask what a result could mean and how follow-up would work.

content.heading: Use local clinical advice
paragraphs: This article does not provide a screening schedule. A qualified local health professional can explain services available in your area and help you decide on next steps.

title: How survivor stories are shared: consent and context
summary: An editorial placeholder explaining consent and context; it is not a personal survivor story.
author: CareGuide Editorial Team

content.heading: No personal story is included in this sample
paragraphs: This is an editorial placeholder, not a first-person account. A real person's story must not be added or published unless that person has given written permission for the specific use.

content.heading: Consent and context
paragraphs: Before publishing a story, confirm permission for the words and identifying details that will appear, explain where the story will be shared, and respect a request not to publish. A consented story should be clearly labeled as shared with permission.

content.heading: Every experience is individual
paragraphs: Each person's experience is unique and is not typical for everyone. A personal account cannot predict another person's diagnosis, treatment, side effects or outcome. For individual concerns, speak with a qualified health professional.
